summary: Gives recommendations for software that automatically responds to email, such as vacation replies and mail filters. It aims to discourage behavior that causes mail loops or floods, for example replying to mailing lists or to messages that were themselves automatic.

eli5.summary: An away-from-desk auto-reply should be polite and not start an endless ping-pong with another robot. This document gives rules so robots behave.

questions: how should vacation auto replies work
out of office email best practices
how to avoid email auto reply loops
where should an out of office reply be sent
subtitle: Rules for vacation replies and other mail robots so they stay useful and never start mail loops.

tldr.problem: Programs that automatically answer email, such as vacation responders and filters, were producing unwanted replies, sending to wrong addresses and sometimes causing mail loops.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC says when responders should stay silent, how to build the response header, content and envelope, where to send it, and defines an Auto-Submitted header field that marks machine-made mail.
tldr.outcome: Responders that follow it send fewer, shorter and better-addressed replies, and other software can recognize and skip automatic mail. It was later updated by RFC 5436.

today: RFC 3834 is a Proposed Standard that was updated by RFC 5436; it has not been obsoleted. The text gives no adoption figures, so this page makes no claim about how widely it is followed.

sections.title: What Counts as an Automatic Response
sections.content:
RFC 3834 recommends behavior for software that answers email without a human, to cut down useless responses, replies to wrong addresses and mail loops, also called sorcerer's apprentice mode: a bug where receiving one message causes several to be sent, each of which triggers the same bug. It is limited to Internet email, and other messaging such as instant messaging, SMS or Usenet was not considered.

The RFC names types of automatic response: delivery status notifications (DSNs), message disposition notifications (MDNs), out of office or vacation notices, change of address notices, challenges, email-based information services and mail filters such as virus scanners. DSNs and MDNs are defined elsewhere, and a response that fits their criteria should follow those specifications instead.

It then groups responders by whom they act for. Service Responders provide a service by email, so the sender expects a reply. Personal Responders act for one recipient, as the UNIX vacation program does. Group Responders act for many recipients, such as a server-wide virus scanner. Personal responders should assume a human reads the reply and send only brief plain text.
sections.eli5: Some email replies come from robots, not people. This document sorts the robots into helpers for one shop, for one person and for a whole town, and gives each polite rules.

sections.title: When Not to Respond
sections.content:
A responder MUST NOT blindly reply to every message. Reasons to hold back include loop prevention, avoiding spam and viruses, not amplifying abuse, not revealing personal information such as that a recipient has not read mail lately, and resisting denial of service.

The guidelines include these:

  • Automatic responses SHOULD NOT be sent to a message with an Auto-Submitted field whose value is anything other than no.
  • Personal and Group responses that say the recipient is away SHOULD NOT repeat to the same sender more than once in several days. A 7-day period is RECOMMENDED as a default.
  • Absence notices SHOULD NOT be sent unless a valid address of the recipient is explicitly in a To, Cc, Bcc, Resent-To, Resent-Cc or Resent-Bcc field.
  • Responders MUST NOT respond when the destination is a null address (SMTP MAIL FROM or Return-Path of <>).
  • Service Responders SHOULD NOT answer extremely malformed requests, and SHOULD NOT return large responses (more than a few kilobytes) without knowing the request was authorized, because return addresses are easily forged.

A responder MAY also skip mail that looks like list traffic, such as a Precedence field of list or any List-* field. Personal and Group Responders MAY reply only to known or trusted correspondents.
sections.eli5: A robot must not answer everything. It should not answer other robots, answer the same person again and again in a week, or answer mail that was not really meant for its owner.

sections.title: Format of a Response
sections.content:
The header is set field by field. From should identify who the response is for: a Service Responder uses an address that reaches the human maintainer and a display name for the service; a Personal Responder uses the recipient's name and an address the recipient chooses, and MUST let the recipient set it; a Group Responder uses the maintainer's address, not Postmaster. Reply-To is set only if a reply is expected. To should name one recipient. Date is when the response was generated.

The Subject should briefly say it is automatic, and the prefix Auto: followed by a space MAY be used before the original subject. Software SHOULD NOT assume that a leading Auto: proves a message is automatic. The response also gets In-Reply-To and References if the original had a Message-ID, and Auto-Submitted: auto-replied.

Personal and Group responses SHOULD be brief text/plain, SHOULD NOT include significant content from the original, and SHOULD NOT include its attachments or non-text content.

In the SMTP envelope the MAIL FROM address SHOULD make loops unlikely, and <> MAY be used. It is RECOMMENDED to specify NOTIFY=NEVER on RCPT if the server supports the DSN option.
sections.eli5: An auto-reply should wear a name tag saying a machine sent it, be short and plain, and tell the post office not to send it back if it cannot be delivered.

sections.title: Where to Send Responses
sections.content:
Automatic responses SHOULD go to the Return-Path if generated after delivery. If generated before delivery they go to the reverse-path from the SMTP MAIL FROM command. If Return-Path is missing after delivery, the responder SHOULD NOT guess another address; it is better to fix the mail delivery system.

Personal and Group Responders SHOULD NOT use Reply-To, From or Sender as the destination. A human sender may set Reply-To to point at a whole mailing list, From may list several addresses, and Sender need not hold a valid reply address, so a robot could reach many people or feed a loop. The RFC calls Return-Path the only address from the message that can be expected, by protocol, to suit unanticipated automatic responses.

A Service Responder MAY send to another address from the request, but only if the service's own specification defines this precisely, and it SHOULD NOT use Reply-To.
sections.eli5: A reply goes to the return address stamped on the envelope. It does not go to a name written inside the letter, because a human may have written that for other humans.

sections.title: The Auto-Submitted Header Field
sections.content:
The Auto-Submitted field marks mail from an automatic process rather than a human, so that filters can keep such mail out of paths where it is unwanted. A message may carry at most one. Its value is no, auto-generated, auto-replied or an extension token, optionally with parameters.

auto-generated is for mail from automatic, often periodic, processes such as UNIX cron jobs that are not direct responses to other messages. It MUST NOT be used for manually generated mail, for direct responses, or for DSNs, MDNs and other delivery reports. The RFC notes some widely deployed SMTP implementations use it for non-delivery reports and should change to auto-replied.

auto-replied SHOULD be used on messages sent in direct response to another message by an automatic process, and MAY be used on DSNs and MDNs. The keyword no MAY explicitly say a human wrote the message. The field SHOULD NOT be added to manually submitted mail, though user agents should not stop a human from setting it for testing.

New keywords must be published as RFCs under IETF Consensus, and names starting with x- are reserved for experiments. Implementations MUST NOT fail on a valid field with optional parameters, but MAY ignore the parameters.
sections.eli5: The header is a sticker on the envelope saying a robot, not a person, wrote this. Robots then know not to answer it.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC lists the attacks that responders enable: relaying or laundering harmful content such as worms, viruses and spam; denial of service by multiplying messages to many addresses or flooding one mailbox; mail loops; probing whether addresses are valid; learning personal information such as recent mailbox activity; and attacking the responder itself with many requests.

The recommendations that reduce these risks are to avoid relaying significant content from the original, mark replies with Auto-Submitted: auto-replied, limit how often one person is answered, respond to at most one address per message, and keep Personal and Group replies brief and plain text. Because email addresses are easily forged, attacks remain possible for any responder that does not limit access and require authentication before replying. These measures limit damage but cannot entirely prevent attacks.
sections.eli5: Bad people can trick a robot into spamming someone or telling secrets. Keeping its replies short, rare and clearly marked helps, but it cannot stop every trick.

items.label: Human origin
items.desc: MAY be used to say a human originated the message.

items.label: Automatic process
items.desc: Periodic or automatic mail that is not a direct reply, such as a cron job. Not for DSNs or MDNs.

items.label: Automatic response
items.desc: SHOULD be used on messages sent by an automatic process in direct response to another message.
